incorrigible

in-KOR-i-juh-bul · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Incorrigible is incapable of being reformed.

Every teacher warned the new principal about the incorrigible prankster in seventh grade who had never once stopped despite years of detentions.

Example

The shelter labeled the old dog incorrigible after it chewed through its fifth leash in a single month, but the new owners just called it spirited.

Incorrigible describes a habit or behavior so persistent that punishment and correction have simply stopped working.

Your Turn

Answer correctly to continue.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

unreformable: Unreformable is the plain label for someone or something not capable of being changed for the better. Incorrigible carries the whole history behind that verdict: every scolding, punishment, and correction has already been tried, and the behavior keeps coming back anyway.

hardened: Hardened describes a person toughened and set in their ways by long experience — a hardened criminal whom nothing shocks anymore. Incorrigible points at the failure of correction itself: no punishment or discipline, however patient, ever changes the behavior for long.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

reformable: capable of being improved

obedient: willing to follow rules

Where it sits · how resistant to change the behavior is — mischievous → incorrigible → irredeemable

mischievous vs. incorrigible: Mischievous is far milder than incorrigible: a mischievous kid teases his sister once for the fun of it, and a single scolding usually ends it.

irredeemable vs. incorrigible: Irredeemable goes a step beyond incorrigible: an incorrigible student defeats every correction, but calling someone irredeemable gives up on the person entirely — beyond saving, not just beyond discipline.
